tldr: We propose a method that drastically self-improves robot policies offline from naturally accumulated mixed-quality deployment experience—including successes and failures—without additional human corrections or exploratory interactions, using chunk-level evaluation with future prediction and quality-conditioned diffusion policies.
hero_caption: Overall framework of the proposed method, PACL. From human demonstrations and mixed-quality autonomous deployment logs, a chunk-level critic equipped with latent dynamics prediction is trained, and a diffusion actor is conditioned and fine-tuned using quality labels derived from the critic's Q-values.
overview:
When a robot policy trained on human demonstrations (such as visual imitation learning) is deployed in real-world environments, it naturally accumulates a large amount of rollouts containing not only successes, but also partial progress and complete failures. While these operational logs are valuable sources of data, directly retraining policies on them using conventional imitation learning risks copying bad behaviors, whereas filtering down strictly to successful data tends to merely rehash what the robot can already do. On the other hand, applying offline reinforcement learning is notoriously difficult because image-based visual-motor control suffers from sparse rewards (only at task completion) and skewed data coverage, leading to highly unreliable value estimation.

To address this, the authors propose Predictive Action Chunk Learning (PACL), a practical post-deployment training framework that relies solely on naturally accumulated deployment logs and sparse task completion labels, without any additional human interventions or real-world trial-and-error exploration. PACL has two core ideas. First, it introduces a chunk-level critic that evaluates temporally extended action sequences (action chunks) while performing an auxiliary task of predicting future latent state changes, creating rich visual feedback to discern good behaviors from bad even under sparse rewards. Second, it uses the learned critic's Q-values to assign discrete quality labels to the data and feeds them as conditioning inputs to a diffusion actor (Diffusion Policy), enabling failed trajectories to be constructively integrated into training as "low-quality behaviors to avoid."

In experiments across four simulation tasks and three real-world Franka arm manipulation tasks, PACL consistently outperformed the pretrained policy as well as strong imitation learning and offline RL baselines. Interestingly, the experiments also demonstrated that discarding failure logs and training only on successful logs actually degraded performance, proving that failure trajectories are indispensable for boosting the critic's discriminative ability.
contributions: Established an offline framework to improve robot policies from naturally accumulated mixed-quality deployment experience without additional human corrections or exploration.
Proposed an action-chunk critic augmented with future latent dynamics prediction, enabling accurate evaluation of high-dimensional action sequences even under sparse rewards.
Developed a technique to construct discrete quality conditions from chunk Q-values to guide diffusion model training, safely and effectively leveraging all trajectories, including failures.
Demonstrated consistent performance gains over strong imitation learning and offline reinforcement learning baselines across four simulation tasks and three real-world setups.

sections.heading: How can we reuse raw logs accumulated by robots in the field?
sections.summary: Robots trained via human demonstrations accumulate diverse successes and failures after deployment, but directly feeding them into imitation learning or offline RL struggles to yield improvements. This paper proposes PACL, a new method that self-improves policies using only deployment logs without requiring human intervention or environment resets.
sections.details:
Imitation learning on large-scale human demonstration datasets has propelled robot manipulation policies forward. However, collecting human demonstrations is extremely expensive, and it is impossible to anticipate all real-world disturbances and uncertainties upfront. Therefore, there is a strong demand to continually enhance policies by reusing the data that deployed robots autonomously accumulate during daily operations—logs that capture clean successes, near-misses, and outright failures.

Yet, because these operational logs are of mixed quality, they cannot simply be thrown back into training. Relying solely on successful trajectories repeats what the robot can already do and provides little new learning signal. Conversely, discarding imperfect rollouts throws away crucial lessons on "what not to do." One might consider using offline reinforcement learning (offline RL) to propagate values backward from both successes and failures; however, in visual-motor setups with sparse rewards given only upon task completion, identifying which action sequences triggered a failure becomes exceedingly difficult, often resulting in performance worse than simple imitation baselines.

Against this backdrop, this work introduces Predictive Action Chunk Learning (PACL), a practical post-deployment training approach that requires zero human intervention or trial-and-error exploration. PACL combines a critic that evaluates temporally extended action sequences (action chunks) while predicting future latent state transitions with a diffusion actor conditioned on chunk Q-values, safely and effectively leveling up the robot's skills from messy deployment logs.

sections.heading: Learning from mixed data: from imitation filtering to reinforcement learning
sections.summary: Existing methods for mixed-quality data fall into imitation-based weighting/filtering approaches and offline RL value-learning approaches. PACL occupies a unique position by leveraging entire deployment logs offline via RL-based principles without complex trajectory slicing or additional human intervention.
sections.details:
Approaches for learning from datasets that include low-quality rollouts broadly divide into two streams:

- **Imitation learning-based approaches (weighting and filtering)**: These methods adjust the influence of transitions by estimating demonstrator or transition reliability, or filter out low-quality sub-trajectories that deviate from expert behavior. For example, recent robotics literature includes SSDF, which uses self-supervised representations to extract and weight useful segments from failure trajectories, and S2I, which uses contrastive learning to select high-quality windows. However, these methods focus primarily on extracting "clean positive data," completely discarding the negative feedback and delayed causal signals embedded in the actions that led to failure.
- **Offline reinforcement learning (Offline RL)**: These methods learn a value function (Q-function) from both successful and failed transitions, propagating long-term outcomes via temporal difference (TD) learning. Frameworks such as DQL and IDQL (which leverage diffusion models for action representation) and RISE (which regularizes around demonstration behaviors to stitch failure rollouts into recovery paths) have been developed. However, in visual manipulation settings with uncontrolled autonomous data coverage, per-step value estimation is prone to collapse, often failing to deliver anticipated gains.
- **Post-deployment improvement with additional intervention**: Other strategies rely on human interventions during failures to provide recovery trajectories or run online RL directly on physical hardware, but these assume ongoing labor costs or safe, automated environment resets.

In contrast, PACL requires no human involvement or active exploration. It reliably estimates values from fixed, accumulated logs by pairing chunk-level evaluation with latent prediction, serving both diffusion actor retraining and test-time candidate reranking.

sections.heading: Inside PACL: chunk evaluation, future prediction, and Q-conditioning
sections.summary: PACL first trains a critic that evaluates action sequences as a whole while predicting future latent representations. It then determines discrete quality labels from these Q-values to train a conditioned diffusion actor, selecting the best candidate chunk at inference time.
sections.details:
### III-A Problem Formulation
We consider a Diffusion Policy (DP) that receives visual observations $o_t$ and proprioceptive robot states $s_t$, taking an observation history of $H_o=2$ steps to output an action chunk $A_t$ consisting of $H_a=8$ continuous action steps. An initial policy $\pi_{\theta_0}$ pretrained on human demonstrations $\mathcal{D}_h$ is deployed in the environment to autonomously collect operational rollouts. Trajectories reaching the task goal are labeled successes $\mathcal{D}_s$, and incomplete ones are labeled failures $\mathcal{D}_f$, forming the full dataset $\mathcal{D} = \mathcal{D}_h \cup \mathcal{D}_s \cup \mathcal{D}_f$. No human interventions or reward engineering are used; only a sparse terminal reward (1 for success, 0 for failure) is provided at episode completion.

### III-B Predictive Action Chunk Critic
Learning values over single-step transitions $(s_t, a_t)$ as in standard RL introduces a mismatch with diffusion models that output temporally coordinated action sequences. PACL instead defines a chunk Q-function $Q_\phi(z_t, A_t)$ and a state value function $V_\psi(z_t)$ that take the entire action chunk $A_t$ as input, trained via expectile regression based on Implicit Q-Learning (IQL).

However, action chunks have very high action dimensionality, and rewards consist only of sparse terminal scalars. To give the critic the fidelity needed to distinguish subtle action qualities, PACL introduces an **auxiliary latent dynamics prediction task**. For an arbitrary prediction horizon $h$ within the chunk, the first $h$ actions $\widetilde{A}_t^{(h)}$ are passed to predict the future latent state change $\Delta z_{t,h} = f_{\bar{\xi}}(o_{t+h}, s_{t+h}) - z_t$. Optimizing this prediction loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{dyn}}$ alongside the critic's TD error encourages the encoder to capture action-conditioned visual features, significantly stabilizing value estimation.

### III-C Actor Training and Inference via Q-Conditioning
Directly imitating low-quality behaviors is detrimental, so PACL constructs quality conditions for the actor using the critic's Q-values. In IQL, the state value $V$ fits an upper expectile of $Q$, resulting in an exceptionally strong correlation between $V$ and $Q$ across the dataset (see Figure F3). Rather than relying on complex metrics like advantage ($Q-V$), PACL uses percentiles of the chunk Q-value distribution itself (the lower 40th percentile as $\delta_l$ and the upper 60th percentile as $\delta_u$) to assign discrete quality labels $c_t \in \{0, 1, \varnothing\}$.

A lightweight conditioning adapter is added to the actor. Human demonstrations $\mathcal{D}_h$ are always labeled $c_t=1$, while intermediate ambiguous data $c_t=\varnothing$ are treated as unconditional, fine-tuning the model with the diffusion noise prediction loss. At inference time, the condition is fixed to $c_t=1$ (high quality) to sample $N=12$ candidate action chunks, and the trained critic selects the chunk with the highest predicted value for execution (see Figure F2).

captions.F3: Correlation analysis between state value $V$ and chunk Q-value in the Square task. Across both successful and failed rollouts, they track each other with a very high correlation ($r>0.95$), demonstrating that raw Q-values effectively serve as a clean quality metric.

sections.heading: Experimental results: dramatic gains across simulation and physical hardware
sections.summary: Evaluated on four Robomimic tasks and three physical Franka tasks, PACL outperformed both imitation learning and offline RL baselines. In-depth ablations highlight the critical roles played by the predictive critic, Q-conditioning, and failure data itself.
sections.details:
### IV-A Experimental Setup
For simulation, four tasks of varying difficulty were selected from the Robomimic benchmark: Can, Transport, Square, and ToolHang. For each task, a DP pretrained on 200 human demonstrations was deployed to collect 500 autonomous rollouts (a mix of successes and failures) as supplementary training data. For real-world experiments, three manipulation tasks (PickCup, StackCup, MoveSpoon) were built using a 7-DoF Franka Panda arm (Figure F4), utilizing 50 human teleoperation demonstrations and 50 autonomous deployment logs per task. PACL was compared against SUB (BC on all data), Self-Imitation (BC on successful logs only), SSDF (filtering valuable segments from failure logs), as well as representative offline RL algorithms: DQL, IDQL, and RISE.

### IV-B Main Results
PACL achieved the top performance across all simulation and real-world tasks, outperforming both the pretrained model and all baselines. For instance, in the challenging Transport simulation task, where the pretrained DP scored 78.8%, SUB degraded to 76.0%, and the strongest imitation baseline SSDF reached 86.4%, PACL achieved an impressive 96.0% success rate. In Square, performance jumped from 80.0% (pretrained) to 93.2%. Real-world evaluations showed similarly consistent superiority across all tasks. Notably, PACL achieves this without complex trajectory slicing or segment filtering like SSDF, relying solely on simple terminal success labels and Q-conditioning.

### IV-C Key Findings from Ablation Studies
- **Component Contributions**: Adding the "Q-conditioned actor" to SUB yielded substantial performance gains, and adding "critic-based candidate selection" at inference provided a clear second boost.
- **Critic Architecture Comparison**: On the Transport task, increasing candidate count $N$ on a standard single-step critic caused scores to plummet due to value misestimation. In contrast, PACL's critic—combining chunk evaluation with latent dynamics prediction—remained robust, maintaining high success rates even as $N$ grew.
- **Conditioning Strategy Comparison**: On Square, PACL's Q-conditioning using Q-value percentiles (91.2%) outperformed Source conditioning based on human vs. autonomous data (85.6%), Outcome conditioning based purely on success/failure (88.0%), and $Q-V$ advantage conditioning (88.8%).
- **Impact of Data Composition**: When training PACL strictly on successful data, the critic could not learn what constituted bad behavior, dropping success on Square to 77.6%. Adding just 50 failure rollouts boosted the score to 88.0%, proving that failure logs provide a critical supervisory signal for value learning.

sections.heading: Conclusion: turning routine operational logs into fuel for autonomous improvement
sections.summary: PACL unites a predictive chunk critic with a Q-conditioned diffusion actor, establishing a powerful method to self-improve robot policies offline from messy, naturally accumulated operational logs. It also reveals that failure data is key to reliable value learning.
sections.details:
This work introduced PACL, a method for robots to self-improve their policies entirely offline using the mixed-quality operational logs naturally accumulated after deployment, without requiring human corrections or real-world exploration.

PACL trains an action-chunk critic enhanced with future latent state prediction, using discrete quality conditions derived from its Q-values to fine-tune a diffusion model. Comprehensive experiments across simulated and physical robot manipulation setups demonstrated clear performance advantages over existing imitation learning and offline reinforcement learning techniques. Ablation studies further underscored the utility of the latent prediction task and highlighted how failure logs are indispensable for fostering the critic's discriminative power.

These findings chart a path toward safely transforming routine daily robot operations into a rich data stream for autonomous continual learning, eliminating the need for dedicated data collection phases.

takeaways: Rather than being discarded, failure data serves as an essential supervisory signal that teaches the critic where the boundary between good and bad actions lies.
When applying reinforcement learning to action chunks, using future latent state prediction as an auxiliary task is highly effective at stabilizing evaluation in high-dimensional action spaces.
For fine-tuning diffusion policies, simple discrete conditioning based on chunk Q-value percentiles proves far more practical and accurate than complex advantage weighting.
limitations: The approach assumes binary labels (sparse rewards) indicating ultimate task success or failure are accurately assigned to each rollout, presenting challenges for ambiguous tasks where outcomes are hard to verify.
Generating $N=12$ candidate action chunks from the diffusion model and evaluating them with the critic at inference time increases computational overhead and inference latency.
Performance may be constrained if deployment rollouts drift drastically from the pretrained policy's behavior distribution, or when learning from initial states that yield zero successful attempts.
